title: Build vs Buy: Should You Build Your Own Design System Platform With AI?
summary: Build vs buy for your design system platform in 2026: what building with Claude Code or Cursor really involves, what Supernova replaces, and how to decide.
body_markdown:
"Couldn't we just build this ourselves?"


Someone on your team has asked it, and they have a point. With Claude Code or Cursor, an engineer can stand up tokens, a docs site, a context file and an MCP server in about a week. We've[written the guide to doing exactly that](https://www.supernova.io/blog/how-to-build-a-design-system-with-ai) .


So the build vs buy design system question has changed. Nobody is weighing a platform against a quarter of engineering work any more. You're weighing it against a week of building and an open-ended amount of running. This guide covers both sides, the layers people tend to forget, and how to decide.


One thing first. Your components stay in your code either way. The choice is whether you build and run the platform around them yourselves: the token sync, the docs, the agent access and the signals that tell you something drifted.


## When building it yourself makes sense


Building is the right call more often than vendors admit. It tends to fit when:


- **The system is small:** one brand, one platform, a handful of consuming teams, and one person who can hold all of it in their head.
- **You've already built it and it works:** if the setup is live and nobody is losing time to it, the cheapest option is to leave it alone.
- **Code is your only source of truth:** if design lives in the code and Figma is a sketchpad, there's less to sync and less to drift.
- **You need total control:** a custom docs experience, unusual hosting rules, or a pipeline nobody else would build.
- **Git already does the job:** versioning, review and history are things Git does well, and a DIY system gets them for free.


If that's you, build it. Use the guide above, keep the context file short, and turn your important rules into lint checks.


## What you're actually signing up to build


Most build estimates price the parts you can see on day one. These are the layers that turn up afterwards, roughly in the order teams meet them.


**1. Getting tokens out of Figma.** Exporting variables once is easy. Syncing them on every change is a pipeline. The[Figma Variables REST API](https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/variables/) requires a full seat in an Enterprise org, so on any other plan someone runs a plugin export by hand, and the copy in your repo is only as fresh as their memory.


**2. A docs site people actually use.** A static site is a day's work. Live component previews, token tables that update themselves and search across both are a product. When[IFC](https://www.supernova.io/blog/creating-a-single-entry-point-for-ifcs-multi-brand-design-system-iceberg) weighed it up, the alternative to a platform was hiring two or three dedicated developers to build and maintain the site.


**3. An MCP server that keeps up.** Your first server takes a day. Then the protocol moves. The[current MCP specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/versioning) , dated 28 July 2026, replaced the initialisation handshake used by every revision up to November 2025 with per-request version negotiation. A homegrown server needs someone to notice that and handle both.


**4. Context per team.** One context file works for one team. With three teams on two frameworks, you either keep one long file that agents[half ignore](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices) or several hand-scoped ones that drift apart.


**5. Knowing what agents get wrong.** A DIY setup has no signal for the lookup that came back empty or the component an agent rebuilt because it couldn't find yours. You find out from a screenshot in review.


**6. Access for people and agents.** Contractors, partner teams and agents all need different slices. In a repo, that's whatever your Git permissions allow.


None of these is hard on its own. Together they're a product, and a product needs an owner. We covered[where that owner's time goes](https://www.supernova.io/blog/hidden-maintenance-cost-diy-design-system) in more detail.


## Build vs buy, layer by layer


Layer Build with AI Keep it running yourself With Supernova


Components Your code Your code Your code, imported, not rebuilt


Tokens from Figma A day, plus an export script Every Figma change, by hand or Enterprise API Synced from Figma as data


Docs site Days for a basic one A site to host, search and keep in sync Generated from the system data


MCP server About a day Spec changes, new tools, keeping data fresh Built in, on every plan


Context per team One file Several files that drift apart Scoped contexts per team and brand


Skills and conventions Repo skills They work well Bring the skills you already wrote


Agent and adoption signal Not included Build your own logging Analytics on lookups and gaps


Versioning Git Git Versions, history and rollback


The left two columns are honest. Agents made the first column cheap. They did much less for the second.


## When buying makes sense


Buying makes sense when the second column has become someone's part-time job, or is about to. The usual triggers are a second brand, a third consuming team, a designer who renames things on a Thursday, or the person who built the MCP server moving teams.


It's also where most teams worry they'll lose what they built. With[Supernova](https://www.supernova.io/compare/diy) you don't:


- **Your components stay in your code:** Supernova imports them from code and Storybook and doesn't ask you to rebuild anything.
- **Your agents and skills stay put:** Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or Copilot keep working as they do now. They read the design system over MCP instead of from a file.
- **The plumbing moves:** Figma sync, the docs site, the MCP server, scoped contexts and the analytics become the product's job rather than a person's.


The trade is real. You pay a subscription, and you give up control over how the plumbing works. In return, the hours in the second column go back to the work your team was hired for. IFC's design system manager[described](https://www.supernova.io/blog/creating-a-single-entry-point-for-ifcs-multi-brand-design-system-iceberg) the result as "a complete and sophisticated documentation site" without the extra developers.


The most common answer is hybrid anyway. You keep building the things that make your system yours, and you stop owning the pipes between them.


## What it costs either way


A subscription is a line item with a renewal date, so it's the number that gets questioned. The DIY cost is the owner's time, spread across token fixes, context rewrites and MCP upkeep, and nobody adds it up.


To see both as numbers, use the[ROI calculator](https://www.supernova.io/roi) . Pick the "already built" option if you have a DIY system today, so build costs count as spent. Then switch to the conservative setting, which assumes your system works exactly as well as Supernova does. Whatever gap is left is the cost of owning it. Plans and limits are on the[pricing page](https://www.supernova.io/pricing) .


## A quick way to decide build or buy


Go down the list and count which column you land in more often.


If this is true… Lean towards


One brand, one platform, under five consuming teams Build


Your current setup works and costs nobody real time Build, or keep what you have


Figma is a sketchpad and code is the source of truth Build


You have a second brand or platform, or one is coming Buy


Tokens reach code only when someone remembers to export them Buy


More than one team's agents read the same context file Buy


One person knows how the MCP server works Buy


You can't say what your agents looked up and didn't find Buy


If most of your answers say build, build, and come back to this list when the next brand or team arrives. If most say buy, you've already paid for the platform once in someone's time, and you can[compare the two options side by side](https://www.supernova.io/compare/diy) .


If you'd rather see the buy column before deciding, this five-minute walkthrough covers each layer from the table: Figma sync, docs, code automation, adoption analytics, and the contexts and MCP your agents read from.
